author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Brown University researcher Dr. Meagan Barry has received a National Institutes of Health award to investigate how a mother’s health may alter microRNAs in human milk and affect infant development. Barry is an assistant professor of emergency medicine and co-chair of the Brown Center for Global Health Equity’s research subcommittee.

Human milk contains microRNAs, small molecules that help regulate gene activity, but researchers still have limited evidence about how maternal conditions change those molecules or what the changes mean for infants. Barry’s project will use samples and data from women and children in the Philippines, focusing on mothers who are underweight or have parasitic infections and measuring infant weight gain and immune maturity.

The award, identified by NIH as 1K08HD118259-01A1, supports an early-career research program linking maternal health, milk biology and child outcomes. Brown faculty Jeffrey Bailey and Jennifer Friedman are serving as co-mentors. The work could help clarify why breastfeeding benefits vary across settings and whether specific biological pathways could guide future nutrition or public-health interventions, particularly where maternal infections and undernutrition are common.
dek: Dr. Meagan Barry will examine how maternal health conditions may change microRNAs in human milk and influence infant growth and immune development.
headline: Brown researcher wins NIH grant to study human-milk microRNAs
